faq.question: What is the difference between linear, radial, and conic gradients?
faq.answer: Linear gradients transition colors along a straight line defined by an angle (e.g., 135deg goes from top-left to bottom-right). Radial gradients spread outward from a center point in circular or elliptical shapes. Conic gradients rotate around a center point like a color wheel, with the angle controlling where the first color starts.

faq.question: What does the repeating gradient option do?
faq.answer: A repeating gradient repeats the color stop pattern rather than filling the entire element. For example, repeating-linear-gradient(90deg, red, blue 20px) produces alternating 20px stripes. Use repeating gradients for patterns like stripes, checkerboards, and progress bars.

faq.question: Can I use more than three color stops?

faq.question: Do CSS filters affect page performance?
faq.answer: CSS filters are GPU-accelerated in modern browsers and generally perform well. However, combining multiple filters with large blur values on high-resolution images can cause rendering slowdowns on mobile devices. For best performance, keep blur values under 10px and avoid applying filters to very large elements.
faq.question: Can I animate CSS filters with transitions or keyframes?
faq.answer: Yes, CSS filters are animatable properties. You can use transition: filter 0.3s ease for hover effects or include filter values in @keyframes animations. Common animated effects include blur-on-hover image reveals and grayscale-to-color transitions on cards.

faq.question: How do I create a neon text effect with CSS text-shadow?
faq.answer: Neon text uses multiple shadow layers with the same color at increasing blur radii. Start with the Neon Glow preset, which uses three layers: a tight white inner glow (0px 0px 4px #fff), a medium-colored glow (0px 0px 8px #0ea5e9), and a wide outer glow (0px 0px 16px #0ea5e9). Stack more layers with larger blur values for a stronger neon effect.

faq.question: Can I animate text shadows for a pulsing glow effect?
faq.answer: Yes. Text shadows can be animated with CSS @keyframes. After generating the base text-shadow value here, wrap it in a @keyframes rule that alternates between the normal shadow and a version with larger blur and brighter colors. Apply the animation to your text element with animation: pulse-glow 2s ease-in-out infinite.

faq.question: Why do my text shadows look different on different browsers?

faq.question: What is the difference between ease, ease-in, ease-out, and linear?
faq.answer: ease (the default) starts slow, speeds up in the middle, and slows down at the end. ease-in starts slow and accelerates. ease-out starts fast and decelerates. linear maintains a constant speed throughout. For UI transitions, ease-out feels responsive. For looping animations like spin, linear prevents unnatural speed changes.

faq.question: When should I use animation-fill-mode: forwards?
faq.answer: Use forwards when you want the animated element to keep its final keyframe state after the animation ends. For example, a fade-in animation should leave the element at opacity: 1. Without forwards, the element would snap back to opacity: 0. For looping animations (infinite), fill mode is usually unnecessary.

faq.question: Can I combine multiple animations on the same element?
faq.answer: Yes, CSS supports multiple comma-separated animations on one element. For example, animation: fadeIn 0.6s ease, pulse 1.2s ease-in-out 0.6s infinite. After generating individual animations here, combine them manually in your CSS by separating each animation shorthand with a comma.

faq.question: What is the difference between perspective and transform: perspective()?
faq.answer: perspective (applied to the parent) creates a shared 3D space where all children share the same vanishing point. transform: perspective() (applied to the element itself) gives each element its own perspective. Use parent perspective when you want multiple 3D elements to share the same viewpoint, like a card flip grid. Use the transform function for standalone 3D effects.

faq.question: Why does my 3D transformed element look flat?
faq.answer: For nested 3D transforms to work, the parent must have transform-style: preserve-3d. Without it, children flatten into the parent's 2D plane. The Preserve 3D checkbox in this tool toggles that property. Also, perspective must be on a parent element, not the transformed element itself — the tool handles this correctly.

faq.question: Do 3D CSS transforms work on all browsers?
faq.answer: 3D transforms are supported in all modern browsers (Chrome 36+, Firefox 49+, Safari 9+, Edge 12+). However, Safari has occasional rendering bugs with nested preserve-3d and overflow: hidden combinations. Test complex 3D layouts across browsers.
